summary.title: Agent Distraction
summary.idea: Stale TODO(bug/...) comments lure coding agents into closed or out-of-scope tickets, wasting steps and tokens; agents that verify a TODO is obsolete and delete it keep the codebase from distracting them.
howItWorks: Use TODO(bug/...) comments as a measurable proxy: log each one an agent reads and whether it then acts on that bug.
Cross-reference each encountered TODO against the ticket's status and the user's prompt to separate valid work from detours.
Unprompted detours cost about 70% more steps, 77% more tokens and 105% more wait time per session.
A cleanup agent checks the history of the bug, the file and surrounding changes, and confirms the TODO's intent is obsolete.
Only confirmed-obsolete TODOs get a deletion change sent for human review, reaching over 95% acceptance.
summary.stealThis: Before your next big agent-assisted task, grep for TODO/FIXME comments that reference closed tickets and delete them, or add an instruction telling the agent not to act on TODOs the prompt doesn't mention.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running coding agents at scale on a large, old codebase and want data on how stale comments cost tokens and cause scope creep.
summary.quote: What is easy for humans to skim past in code, agents see as a call to action.

verdict.reason: The post teaches a transferable context-hygiene technique, backed by strong session data: find TODO(bug/...) references to closed tickets, then use an agent to check bug and file history before proposing deletion for human review. The card's steal-this oversimplifies it to grep-and-delete and adds an instruction tip the page never gives.

summary.title: Agents Are Going Async
summary.idea: A blocking agent loop makes the user wait on every long task, so split it into an orchestrator that stays reachable and background subagents that report back when done.
howItWorks: The orchestrator starts a subagent on its own thread and the call returns immediately, like an unawaited promise.
Five tools manage tasks: start, check, update, cancel and list, so the orchestrator can steer work in flight.
Follow-ups use an update strategy: interrupt restarts the subagent with a correction, enqueue holds an addition until the run ends.
Unfinished tasks are listed in the orchestrator's system prompt, so it always knows what is in flight.
Results arrive mid-run before a model call, wake an idle orchestrator, or wait while an approval is pending.
summary.stealThis: The next time a slow tool call stalls your agent's conversation, wrap it as a start/check/cancel task triple and list the pending tasks in the system prompt.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building agents whose long tool calls block the conversation and want the exact task tools, update strategies and notification rules.
summary.quote: An async subagent works like a task started with asyncio.create_task or a Promise you don't await yet.

verdict.reason: Partly a Deep Agents feature post, but the async orchestrator pattern is portable: start/check/update/cancel/list task tools, interrupt vs enqueue follow-ups, pending tasks in the system prompt, and busy/idle/approval notification rules. The only code shown is product config, so it scores as thin.

summary.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
summary.idea: Agent-written PR descriptions are accurate but so long that reviewers skip them, so put a short human-curated opener on top and fold the full agent text into a collapsed section.
howItWorks: Start the PR description with a short paragraph a human chose as the fastest way to understand the change.
Add a screenshot or copied command output when a visual shows the feature quickly.
Wrap the full agent-written description in a details element, which GitHub Markdown renders collapsed with an expansion arrow.
Use the model name and effort level, such as 'Claude Opus 5.5 Medium', as the summary label.
If the agent's own text already contains a good opener, lift it out instead of writing a new one.
summary.stealThis: Before opening your next agent-authored PR, keep a one- or two-sentence human-approved opener at the top and paste the agent's full essay inside <details><summary>model name</summary>.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing a steady stream of agent-written PRs and want a cheap way to keep descriptions readable without losing detail.
summary.quote: I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction

verdict.reason: A small, immediately copyable technique for cheaper review: a human-curated opener on top, with the full agent-written PR description folded into <details><summary> labelled with the model name, backed by real PR examples, though it's narrow and light.

summary.title: Reflex: an architecture for building mobile apps with agents
summary.idea: Emulators make agent feedback slow, so Reflex runs app logic headlessly and exposes each screen's state and actions as JSON, letting a CLI and one shared test file drive both iOS and Android.
howItWorks: Keep all non-UI logic in a core module with no UI imports, with platform services passed in through the constructor.
Give every screen's ViewModel the same shape: actions in, state out, one update function that changes state.
Add an introspection node per ViewModel exposing a name, state as JSON, and every action, with no conditionals.
A CLI with ls and do commands reads and drives the focused screen, and the same tests run on both platforms.
Block all network calls in tests and supply fixtures, so a suite of 1,700+ tests runs in about four minutes.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-built feature, add a small JSON state-and-actions interface to one screen or service so the agent can inspect it and run a journey test in a terminal without a UI or device.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building mobile or UI-heavy apps with agents and want a fast, deterministic feedback loop plus one test suite keeping two platforms in parity.
summary.quote: The code is written twice, the tests are written once.

verdict.reason: A detailed, portable architecture for agent feedback loops: a headless core, a strict ViewModel contract, a JSON introspection node exposing state and actions, an ls/do CLI, network-blocking fixtures, and one shared journey test file for both platforms, with explicit build-it-yourself steps and real numbers (1,700+ tests in about four minutes).

summary.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
summary.idea: Line-by-line review can't keep up with agent output, and agent-written tests check what was built, so PDD Kit proves code against a reviewed formal spec and tests only what proofs can't reach.
howItWorks: The agent asks clarifying questions before writing anything, then records answers in a plain-language intent artifact mapped to formal spec clauses.
Code the verifier can't see, like bcrypt or the database, gets a wrapper with an assumed contract the developer signs off individually.
Each assumed clause gets a Given/When/Then test, and results are labelled proof or evidence so readers know what backs each claim.
Reviewer agents critique the spec, then a mutation check plants one bug per clause; the verifier must reject each, exposing clauses that constrain nothing.
CI runs the proof alongside the tests, so any later change by a person or agent must keep satisfying the same spec.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent task on something sensitive like login or permissions, have the agent ask about ambiguities first, and write the requirement both ways (only X gets a token, and X always gets one).
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck reviewing large agent diffs, and want to see how a spec, trust boundary and mutation checks can replace reading the code.
summary.quote: Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?”

verdict.reason: The page teaches portable verification techniques with real Verus code from a worked login example: questions before code, stating requirements in both directions, wrapping trusted dependencies in assumed contracts each backed by a Given/When/Then test, and planting one bug per spec clause to expose clauses that constrain nothing; full proof needs Rust/Verus and the kit is a research prototype.

summary.title: How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
summary.idea: Students can one-shot last year's homework, and engineers drown in agent output; this episode covers teaching the harness itself and checking understanding of agent diffs before review.
howItWorks: Build a coding agent from scratch in about 200 lines, then proxy real Claude Code traffic to read its prompts.
For big codebases, run research, then proposal with a human choosing, then plan/spec, then implementation and tests.
Use an explain-diff skill that gives a visual walkthrough and quizzes you on the change.
Write skills yourself, then run a cutter skill to trim bloat; prune unused skills regularly.
At Monaco, buy tools to learn what you need, then build the ones you keep, like agent workspaces.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-written PR merge, run an explain-diff style skill on the patch and note which quiz question forces you to reopen the code.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're an engineer or lead wanting a tour of a modern agent-coding syllabus and how one team decides what to build versus buy.
summary.quote: You buy to learn, and you build to keep.

verdict.reason: The written intro and transcript give several briefly mentioned techniques you could copy: Geoffrey Litt's explain-diff skill that quizzes you on an agent's patch, intercepting Claude Code traffic with mitmproxy to read its prompts, a research-proposal-plan flow for large codebases, and a skill-cutter skill. Each is only mentioned in passing inside a long, wide-ranging interview, so it falls well short of the bonus-listen bar.

summary.title: Reading a test result out of a coding agent's transcript is harder than checking the exit code
summary.idea: Checking whether an agent's last test run passed by reading one exit code misreads many runs; parsing the command structure, exit codes and summary lines, with a third 'unknown' verdict, gives a trustworthy check.
howItWorks: Split the command on |, &&, || and ; and find the test runner; a pipe to tail makes the exit code unreliable.
Treat exit codes like 124, 126, 127, 128+ and pytest 2-5 as 'no verdict', not a failed test.
Parse the summary line first: strip ANSI colours, drop coverage-gate lines and zero counts, and beware formats like 'passing: 95 failing: 0'.
Keep a third answer, unknown, for runs like 'collected 0 items' or usage errors, and ignore --collect-only runs.
Track git stash and git stash pop so baseline test runs on pre-change code aren't counted as the agent's last run.
summary.stealThis: Before you trust any automated 'did the tests pass' check on agent logs, sample 20 random flagged cases by hand, and wire the Stop hook idea: send the agent back once if its last test run failed and its final message doesn't say so.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building hooks, CI gates or audits that read agent transcripts and need to trust a pass/fail verdict.
summary.quote: Treating that as a pass or a fail is how you get confident nonsense.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable way to judge an agent's last test run, backed by before/after numbers from 16,000 runs and a linked repo: split piped commands, treat timeout and signal exit codes as no verdict, parse summary lines first, keep an 'unknown' answer, track git stash baselines, and hand-check a sample of flagged cases.

summary.title: Stop hook: end the turn when the agent's try fails the same way
summary.idea: A Stop hook that blocks on every failing validate can loop on failures the agent can't fix; now it ends the turn when a retry fails identically and shows the failure to the person.
howItWorks: On Stop, run validate; if it passes, clear any remembered failure and let the turn end.
The first stop of a turn always blocks on failure, so the agent gets one try.
On the next stop (stop_hook_active), compare the failure fingerprint with the last block's fingerprint.
The fingerprint is a sorted set of output lines with durations and percentages stripped, so parallel runners' timings and ordering don't matter.
A match ends the turn with a systemMessage showing the failure; a changed failure keeps blocking. State lives per session in the temp folder.
summary.stealThis: Add a failure-fingerprint check to your Stop hook (normalise timings, sort lines, compare to the previous block) the next time an unfixable failing check makes your agent loop.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running a validate-on-stop hook and watching agents burn minutes re-running checks they can't fix, and want the tests and mutation checks as a template.
summary.quote: pnpm validate failed the same way twice, so the turn ends anyway

verdict.reason: A concrete, portable Stop-hook pattern: block on failing validate, then end the turn when the retry's normalised, sorted failure fingerprint matches, surfacing it via systemMessage. It comes with pseudocode, named tests, before/after results, mutation checks and a live run, but it is a narrow fix inside one PR.

summary.title: mergeproof: evidence gates for pull requests
summary.idea: PR claims like "added tests, verified on staging" cost nothing to type, so mergeproof puts one YAML policy in the repo that CI enforces and agents read to learn what proof to produce.
howItWorks: A policy file pairs a trigger (paths, labels, title) with required checks, such as tests changed or a CI job passing.
Contributors and agents add a fenced evidence block to the PR description with before/after trace links.
CI verifies the proof: tests must be in the diff, jobs green on the head commit, links resolve at source.
Human sign-off is bound to the commit SHA, so a new push invalidates the earlier approval.
Agents run `mergeproof explain` in their loop to see what's missing, then open the PR with the evidence.
summary.stealThis: Add a rule to your repo's agent instructions file that bug-fix PRs must include a fenced evidence block with before/after links, and check it in CI before your next agent-authored fix.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing agent PRs by hand and want a machine-checked definition of done that agents can read and satisfy themselves.
summary.quote: Pull requests earn their merge with evidence, not claims.

verdict.reason: The page teaches a portable, open-source evidence-gate pattern with working config and workflow code: a declarative policy file that both CI and agents read, a machine-readable evidence block in the PR, before/after trace links checked at their source, and human sign-off bound to the commit SHA.

summary.title: Before I Could Evaluate My Coding-Agent Harness, I Had to Isolate It
summary.idea: Comparing agent harness variants is unreliable when config leaks in from your global setup, so the author treats each harness as a versioned profile and runs it in an isolated temporary environment.
howItWorks: Give each run the same repo, starting commit and prompt, so only the harness or model changes.
Store each harness (skills, instruction files, settings, hooks) as a named profile in version control.
Run each profile in a temporary cell with its own HOME, separate from your everyday global config.
Record a trace per run with profile and task digests plus an isolation check, so you know what was loaded.
Keep isolation and evaluation as separate tools, so changing your judging criteria never forces rebuilding the run layer.
summary.stealThis: Before your next harness comparison, check what config the agent actually loaded (for example Claude Code's /status setting sources) and snapshot the harness as a versioned profile instead of editing it in place.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're pruning an accumulated CLAUDE.md or skills setup and want repeatable, trustworthy comparisons across harness variants or models.
summary.quote: A harness becomes a named artifact I can preserve instead of a collection of files I continuously overwrite.

verdict.reason: An honest walkthrough of a real harness comparison, including what went wrong (pstack silently active, config leaking). It teaches a portable technique: snapshot each harness as a versioned profile, run it with an isolated HOME or CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, and check what actually loaded. It is narrow and the evaluation side is left unresolved, so it is thin.

summary.title: docs(github): make the PR template fit agent-written PRs
summary.idea: File-by-file PR templates make agents pad descriptions with diff-repeating lists; reworking the template to ask for design changes, verification evidence and open questions gives reviewers what they need.
howItWorks: Replace the per-file Backend/Frontend change list with changes grouped by what they do, framed as design changes.
Add a pointer for where to start reviewing and which parts can be skimmed.
Add a 'How It Was Verified' section for evidence CI can't produce: evals, manual and end-to-end checks.
Require the author to state what was not verified, with reasons.
Add an 'Open Questions' section for uncertainty and decisions left to the human reviewer.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-authored PR, edit the PR template to include 'How It Was Verified' (including what was skipped) and 'Open Questions' sections in place of file lists.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're reviewing a growing stream of agent-written PRs and want a template that surfaces risk and unverified areas instead of diff-repeating lists.
summary.quote: Agents fill that with long file lists that repeat the diff, while the things a reviewer most needs

verdict.reason: Teaches a copyable PR-template rework for agent-authored PRs: design-grouped changes, a review starting point, a 'How It Was Verified' section that includes what was skipped, and 'Open Questions'. The PR description itself is a worked example, but the full template text isn't shown, so it's thin.

summary.title: AI Agent Guardrails Example: Copy-Paste Claude Code Rules
summary.idea: Unattended coding agents can run destructive commands, loop, overspend or quit early; layered deny rules, blocking hooks and CLI caps give each failure its own deterministic guardrail.
howItWorks: Commit deny rules in .claude/settings.json to block known commands like force pushes and reads of .env files.
A PreToolUse hook reads the command string, matches destructive patterns by regex, and exits with code 2 to block them.
Run headless jobs with --permission-mode dontAsk, --max-turns and --max-budget-usd so loops and spend stay capped.
A tool-call counter hook keyed on session_id denies calls after a set limit as a backstop.
A Stop hook blocks quitting while tests fail, but checks stop_hook_active first to avoid endless bouncing.
summary.stealThis: Before scheduling your next unattended claude -p job, add the block-destructive PreToolUse hook, then test it by asking the agent to run rm -r -f on a throwaway folder.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running coding agents on cron or CI and want copy-paste hook scripts plus a table of what each guardrail layer misses.
summary.quote: Exit code 2 is the way a hook signals 'stop, don't do this'.

verdict.reason: Teaches concrete, copy-paste guardrail layers for unattended Claude Code runs (deny rules, an exit-2 PreToolUse regex hook, max-turns/budget caps, a session tool-call counter, and a Stop hook guarded by stop_hook_active), with scripts, a verification step and a table of what each layer misses; the patterns port to other agent harnesses, though the code is Claude Code-specific.

summary.title: Claude Code Diff Verification in 2026: How to Make Your Agent Assert Its Own Edits Did Not Break the Build
summary.idea: Coding agents declare success without running any check that could prove them wrong. A Stop hook exiting with code 2 on failure forces the agent to fix typecheck, lint and test errors first.
howItWorks: Add a Stop hook command in .claude/settings.json that runs your typecheck, such as tsc --noEmit, and exits 2 on failure.
Exit code 2 blocks the turn from ending and feeds stderr back to the agent, which fixes and retries.
Put several checks in a verify script that exits at the first failure, so the agent gets immediate feedback.
Keep hook checks fast (typecheck, unit tests); leave integration tests and security scans to CI, and run the script by hand first.
Layer weaker checks around it: in-prompt asks, /goal conditions, and a fresh-subagent /code-review for logic the tests miss.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent session, add a Stop hook running `pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2` to .claude/settings.json, so the agent can't finish until types pass.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're tired of finding broken builds after an agent said 'done' and want ready-to-copy hook scripts plus guidance on which checks belong where.
summary.quote: If the command exits with code 2, the turn does not end.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable Stop hook (exit 2 on failed typecheck, lint or tests feeds errors back so the agent must fix them before finishing), with config and scripts and guidance on which checks belong in hooks versus CI, though it is somewhat repetitive and AI-assisted.

summary.title: Harness Engineering Roadmap: Claude Code From First Principles
summary.idea: Harness engineering is hard to learn from the outside, so this roadmap rebuilds a Claude Code-style coding agent in eight steps, from design through sandboxing, context management, evals and failure replay.
howItWorks: Design the harness first: a tiny agent core, six modules, several interfaces, and an evals layer underneath.
Build a bare-bones ReAct loop with nine tools (read, write, edit, bash at the core) and a steering queue.
Run tools in a Docker or Modal sandbox rather than on your host machine.
Keep context small using memory, skills, LSP diagnostics, compaction, and parallel scoped subagents.
Measure with a custom benchmark and hidden verifiers, then freeze past failures into a replayable regression suite.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent change, take a few failed runs, record them with their tool outputs, and replay them after every tweak as a regression suite.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building your own agent harness and want a hands-on, step-by-step course with code, covering sandboxes, context, evals and debugging.
summary.quote: The tools are 90% of why this is a coding agent and not any other kind of AI agent.

verdict.reason: Mostly a course index with a sponsor slot, but it names specific, portable patterns backed by an open-source repo. These include sandboxing only the computer-use tools, compacting at 80%, keeping the eval harness from importing the agent loop, scoring with hidden verifiers, and replaying clustered failed runs with recorded tool outputs.

summary.title: How we rebuilt the Shopify app in 12 weeks
summary.idea: Agents write code faster than humans can check it, so Shopify rebuilt its mobile architecture, tests and review flow so agents get fast feedback and humans only judge intent.
howItWorks: Business logic runs without a device, so agents load a ViewModel from a CLI and check state in milliseconds.
Architecture lives in examples, architecture.md files, lint rules and CI checks that fail when iOS and Android diverge.
The legacy app serves as the spec; work splits into small checkpoints verified against it, not a written spec.
An agent does an adversarial review against the guidelines first; humans then review small cross-platform PRs for intent.
Each day an agent turns that day's review comments into updates to skills and Architecture.md, so one comment becomes a rule.
summary.stealThis: At the end of each day, have an agent read all review comments from your PRs and fold the recurring ones into your skills or architecture.md file.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're scaling agent output and finding that review, CI and merging, not code generation, are now your bottleneck.
summary.quote: Agents need more than instructions. They need a way to discover when they are wrong.

verdict.reason: A real, evidence-backed walkthrough of Shopify's harness: device-free ViewModel checks via CLI, CI divergence gates, the legacy app as spec with small checkpoints, agent-first adversarial review, and a daily agent that folds review comments into skills and Architecture.md, all of which the card reports accurately; the main gap is that it shows no code or concrete files.

summary.title: How our GTM Agent builds consistent, high-quality sales artifacts
summary.idea: Sales reps built proposals and plans by hand, and the results varied. LangChain fixed this by giving an agent templates, stage rules, account data and brand assets, plus a render-and-review loop with a stopping rule.
howItWorks: Skills hold the sales process, templates and stage rules, versioned separately from the code.
The agent reads the CRM record and shared account folder, and asks the rep for any missing inputs.
It copies a leadership-owned template into a sandbox, fills it in, renders to PDF, and inspects the page images.
Self-review stops once one pass finds no real defect, cutting a one-pager run from 18 minutes to 7.
The finished file goes to the rep with flags on parts a human must still fill in.
summary.stealThis: Add a stopping rule to any self-review loop, such as 'ship once one review finds no real defect', the next time your agent produces a document and keeps re-checking pages that are already fine.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building an agent for a non-engineering team and want a worked example of templates, brand rules, review loops and usage metrics.
summary.quote: We spend very little time on prompts that compensate for the model and instead focus on capturing how our business runs.

verdict.reason: Teaches a portable artifact pipeline for a sales team: leadership-owned templates, brand kit baked into the sandbox, and a python-pptx → LibreOffice PDF → rasterized self-review loop with a stopping rule (18 to 7 minutes). There's a product pitch but no code, which keeps it at 7.

summary.title: What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents
summary.idea: Tweaking agent prompts by hand makes it hard to tell if a change helped, so write a pass/fail spec and a failing eval first, then compare experiments after each change.
howItWorks: Write a short spec per behavior: when it triggers, what to do, what not to do, what must keep working.
Build a dataset from real agent runs, and have an LLM rewrite examples to cover missing cases.
Pick a code eval for deterministic checks like tool choice; use an LLM judge only when needed.
Run a baseline experiment before changing anything, then compare each change per example, not just by average.
Open the failing trace to find the cause, and keep a held-out set to catch overfitting.
summary.stealThis: Before adding your next tool to an agent, write a four-line spec (when, do, don't, keep intact), add examples including near-miss negatives, and confirm the eval fails before you build.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're iterating on agent prompts or tools by gut feel and want a repeatable loop to catch regressions in CI and production.
summary.quote: Write it first and confirm it fails on the current broken version.

verdict.reason: The post teaches a portable eval-first loop: a four-part behavior spec, a dataset that covers existing behavior, a baseline run, per-example experiment comparison, trace review and a held-out set. A worked docs-agent example shows a real regression (the VPN how-to question filing a ticket) and its fix, and none of it depends on LangSmith.

summary.title: Tests as data
summary.idea: AI agents rewrite their own tests, so developers stop trusting them; moving the contract into readable data files run by a small AI-generated runner makes tests easy to review and to protect.
howItWorks: Write customer tests as input, expected output and setup in YAML or CSV tables, with no implementation details.
Draft one sample test in your preferred DSL, then have the agent write the parser and test runner.
Use an external DSL where assertions are mandatory syntax, so the agent can't write weak or assertion-free tests.
Protect test data and runner files with read-only permissions, hooks, or a CI check on which files changed per task type.
Validate the tests with mutation testing and an oracle, such as official manuals or a real system running the same tests.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent-written feature, put the acceptance cases in a YAML or CSV table, have the agent build a small runner for it, and fail CI if that data file changes in a refactoring PR.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're letting agents write and refactor tests, no longer trust the suite, and want concrete DSL, runner and file-protection patterns to rebuild that trust.
summary.quote: In short, prose specs can't be executed; tests can.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable technique for protecting agent-written tests: put customer tests in YAML/CSV data files, have the agent generate the runner, and use an external DSL that makes assertions mandatory. It backs this with a task-type table of which files may change, read-only/CI/hook protection, and mutation and oracle validation, all with plenty of code examples.

summary.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
summary.idea: A coding agent can't hear, so the author gave it ears: browser microphones on spare devices stream to a server the agent controls and can hot-patch, letting it iterate unattended.
howItWorks: Start with a problem.md prompt; Claude researches the problem and finds a relevant paper (BeepBeep) before any code is written.
Listener devices open a WebSocket to a Python server, keep a 60-second audio buffer, and flag likely beeps with an FFT detector.
A hot-swap installModule() method lets the server push new JavaScript to every listener without reloading pages or re-granting microphone permission.
A clap mode gives a known test signal, and replayable logs let the human confirm which recording is the target beep.
Features are added through short, plain-English prompts while the author sits by the laptop and chats with the agent.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent task that depends on the physical world, have the agent write a problem.md first, then add a hot-reload channel and a known test signal so it can observe and fix things itself.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building agent setups that need to perceive or debug real-world systems, and want a worked example of a live-patchable feedback loop.
summary.quote: I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it’s possible to give Claude Code ears.

verdict.reason: The post walks through a real build with its actual prompts. It teaches portable techniques: research into a problem.md first, a hot-swap code channel so the agent can redeploy to sensors without human help, and a known test signal (claps) to check the agent's perception. Its use is somewhat narrow to physical-world tasks.

summary.title: Long-horizon agents and durable execution
summary.idea: Agents that run for days or weeks crash, retry and act on stale facts; wrapping the loop in durable execution and putting business rules in tool code lets them recover safely.
howItWorks: Route every outside call (model decision, tool, message) through a logged step; after a crash, replay skips recorded steps and rebuilds state.
Gate tools with an allowed(state) check, so rules like 'no order before approval' live in code, not the prompt.
Use an idempotency key, such as the PO number, so at-least-once retries don't place duplicate orders.
Re-check facts before irreversible actions, and have managers approve a price range with an expiry instead of one value.
Version business rules in state so running tasks finish under the old rule while new ones use the new one.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent tool that does something hard to undo, add a deterministic allowed() precondition and a re-read of the underlying facts inside the tool, rather than trusting the prompt.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building agents that wait on people or external systems for days and need crash recovery, retries and safe deploys.
summary.quote: This way the business rules that matter are in code, not in the prompt.

verdict.reason: Teaches concrete, portable harness patterns with working code: state-gated allowed() tools so rules live in code, logged steps with replay, idempotency keys on retries, re-check-before-commit with approved price ranges, and versioned rules for running tasks.

summary.title: the answer to ai is engineering
summary.idea: Agents hill-climb toward goals and do destructive things, and unit tests miss edge cases. The fix is engineering: remove dangerous capabilities from the environment, add deterministic back pressure, and use property-based tests.
howItWorks: Define packages once in a Nix overlay so laptops, CI, agent sandboxes and Docker images share one source of truth.
Patch tools such as git to remove force push, so the agent cannot do it at all.
Block bad loop output with pre-commit hooks, compile checks and static analysis of domain-coupling rules.
Use property-based testing to explore edge cases, for example reversing a string twice returns the original.
Add a dated AGENTS.md reminder to remove temporary patches, instead of filing a ticket.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent loop, remove a risky capability like force push from the sandbox's git, and add a pre-commit hook that rejects code which fails to compile.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running agent loops in sandboxes and want deterministic guardrails, Nix-based reproducible environments, or property-based testing to cut review load.
summary.quote: The best way to stop a model from doing something is to remove its ability to do it.

verdict.reason: Concrete, transferable guardrail techniques: removing dangerous capabilities by patching tools such as git via a Nix overlay, with a public nix-demo repo as evidence, plus a dated AGENTS.md cleanup reminder, pre-commit and static-analysis back pressure, and property-based tests; the card matches the page, though some of it is talk-style and drifts into Antithesis tools.

summary.title: The AI agent wasn't confused. It was drowning in 200 tools.
summary.idea: An agent sending about 200 tool definitions per call gave wrong answers and burned tokens; retrieving only the 4 or 5 relevant tools per request fixed both.
howItWorks: Log what the agent actually sends to the model on each request before touching the prompt.
Store each tool as a vector row: name, description, example queries, tags and an endpoint.
Embed the user query, run vector search, and pass only the top 4 or 5 tools to the loop.
Run tool implementations behind external endpoints so adding a tool is a new row, not a deployment.
Always include a search tool so the model can retry with a richer query when retrieval misses.
summary.stealThis: The next time an agent picks wrong actions, log the request payload and count tool definitions, then try top-k retrieval of tools plus a fallback tool-search call.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're running an agent with dozens of tools and want a concrete design for retrieving them per request.
summary.quote: Fewer choices beat better descriptions.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, transferable pattern of retrieving top-k tools via vector search per request, with a fallback tool-search tool, backed by a code sketch and a before/after table, though it reports no measured numbers.

summary.title: Your Coding Agent Thinks It Has Finished. Make It Prove It.
summary.idea: Agents declare work done without real proof, so write a Definition of Ready and a Definition of Done, then enforce Done with a Stop hook that blocks finishing until typecheck, lint and tests pass.
howItWorks: Write short docs/definition-of-ready.md and definition-of-done.md files with concrete, command-checkable items, then import them into CLAUDE.md.
A /ready skill with disable-model-invocation interviews you about gaps and writes SPEC.md with runnable acceptance checks.
A Stop hook script runs typecheck, lint and tests, exiting 2 with stderr output so the agent must keep working.
A read-only reviewer subagent compares the diff to SPEC.md in a fresh context, reporting correctness gaps and skipping style.
/goal sets a session-level done condition checked by a separate model, while the hook guarantees the checks actually ran.
summary.stealThis: Before your next unattended agent run, add a Stop hook script that runs your typecheck, lint and test commands and exits 2 on any failure, so the agent can't finish on red.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're letting agents run unattended and want copyable hook, skill and subagent configs that turn 'all tests pass' into evidence.
summary.quote: If you keep adding emphasis to a CLAUDE.md line and Claude still misses it, that's a sign the line belongs in a hook.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable Definition of Ready/Done setup: a /ready skill that writes SPEC.md, a Stop hook script exiting 2 on failing typecheck/lint/tests, and a read-only reviewer subagent, with configs and caveats. It is Claude Code-specific but the pattern ports to other harnesses, and it partly rehashes Anthropic's docs.

summary.title: Inspecting the Harness Before Changing an Agent Behavior
summary.idea: Patching one file when an agent behavior spans several often breaks something else, so bundle every related file, have a second model write the fix prompt, and give that to the agent.
howItWorks: Run one command with a topic, such as 'inspect the harness for how X works'.
The agent gathers instruction-file excerpts, matching skills, scripts, notes and scheduled jobs into one markdown file.
Search ranks filename and heading hits above body mentions, and keeps every file that could influence the behavior.
It prints the file path without summarising anything or changing anything.
Paste the bundle and your complaint into a stronger model, then paste its returned prompt into your agent.
summary.stealThis: Add an 'Inspect the harness' line to your AGENTS.md so the next time an agent behavior keeps regressing after rule patches, you bundle all related files and ask a second model for the fix prompt.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're repeatedly patching skills or instruction files and finding that each fix breaks a different case.
summary.quote: A fix that works 80% of the time is worse than no fix.

verdict.reason: The post teaches a concrete, copyable 'inspect the harness' command that bundles every instruction file, skill, script, note and scheduled job tied to one behavior, then has a second model write the fix prompt. It includes a ready-made setup prompt and an AGENTS.md line, though the evidence is a single anecdote.

summary.title: Every PR gets an agent review before a human sees it
summary.idea: Reading about 50 PRs a week cold is slow, so each PR first goes to a read-only reviewer agent on a different vendor than the author, and a report reaches the human before the diff.
howItWorks: Launch one scout agent per PR in its own pane; each can only read the PR and writes report.md locally.
A binding charter forbids commenting, approving, pushing or merging, and requires findings ordered by severity with file:line citations.
A fifth spec-review pass sees only the diff, commits and ticket, listing what was asked but not built, built but not asked for, built wrong.
Pin the reviewer model explicitly, since role overrides skip scouts, and use a different vendor than the code-writing model.
Cap review rounds at 3 (5 for security changes) and keep a ledger where every finding ends fixed, rejected with reason, or open.
summary.stealThis: Before your next batch of PRs, write a read-only review charter (no posting, cited file:line findings, escalate auth and data changes) and run it on a different model than the one that wrote the code.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck reviewing agent PRs and want the actual charter text, model pinning notes, and tested launcher scripts.
summary.quote: The agent can read the PR and nothing else: it can't comment, approve, push or merge.

verdict.reason: A real setup with code that teaches a portable pre-review pattern: a read-only reviewer agent on a different vendor, run under a verbatim charter (cited file:line findings, auth/data escalation), plus a spec-only pass, a capped review budget and a findings ledger, all backed by real scripts and a tested companion repo.

summary.title: The Guardrails Customers Never See
summary.idea: Customer-facing agents that can act on accounts risk damaging relationships, so design three invisible layers: scoped access, written escalation rules, and kill switches with action logs, instead of trusting the model's judgement.
howItWorks: Scope permissions to specific actions rather than whole systems, and keep read access separate from write access.
Set limits inside each action, such as a refund cap, once per order, for approved reasons; out-of-bounds requests get routed, not refused.
Write escalation rules before launch, covering request type, value thresholds, and signals like repeated requests or frustration.
On handover, pass a summary of the customer's goal, what was tried, and why the agent stopped.
Build per-action kill switches the business can pull, and log each action with its trigger, data used and outcome.
summary.stealThis: Before your next agent gets write access to a customer-facing system, write a one-page spec listing what it can touch, the exact triggers for human handover, and which single action you can pause.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're a non-engineering leader or builder about to let an agent change customer accounts and need a simple permissions and escalation checklist.
summary.quote: Reviewing a sample of agent actions every week is the fastest way to find the rules that need tightening.

verdict.reason: Thin but concrete: it gives a three-layer guardrail checklist for customer-facing agents (action-scoped tools with per-action caps, pre-written escalation triggers with a handover summary, per-action kill switches plus action logs) that teams can copy, though it offers no code or evidence.

summary.title: I stopped babysitting my coding agents. Here's the workflow.
summary.idea: Running many parallel agents left the author as the bottleneck on decisions and bug-finding, so they switched to one owner agent that proves its work on the real app, checked by a different model family.
howItWorks: Interview first: core-grill asks only about user-visible choices, then core-spec writes spec.md and verify.md, with checks written before any code.
A different model family reviews both files read-only in a fresh session; then they are frozen and a draft PR is opened.
One deliver agent owns the work, keeps a committed plan.md in ExecPlan format, and checks each milestone with a fresh subagent.
A script, check-delivery.mjs, gates merge: frozen specs unchanged, report covers merged code, verdict PASS, verifier from another model family.
Decisions and deviations sit at the top of the PR, each noting what to redo if overturned, so the human reviews decisions, not diffs.
summary.stealThis: Before your next multi-step feature, write verify.md scenarios that start from a real user entry point and note what the old code does, so a check that could never fail gets caught.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're the bottleneck on relaying decisions and catching late bugs in agent output, and want a complete, installable spec-verify-deliver loop with cited sources.
summary.quote: When the agent struggles, we treat it as a signal: identify what is missing—tools, guardrails, documentation—and feed it back into the repository.

verdict.reason: A real walkthrough of an audited multi-agent setup that teaches concrete, portable techniques: specs and verify.md written before code and frozen, verification by a different model family, a plan.md in ExecPlan format committed to the repo, and a check-delivery.mjs merge gate, with an open-source repo and before/after evidence.

summary.title: Debates, voting, and reflection loops: composing an agentic PR reviewer that costs less than a dollar
summary.idea: One agentic pattern can't review a large PR cheaply and reliably, so a deterministic pipeline applies routing, debate, voting and reflection only where they pay off, under a cost cap.
howItWorks: A fixed sequence does fetching, validating, calibrating and rendering in plain code; model judgment sits only inside specific steps.
A routing step picks which of five specialist reviewers run, and a deterministic floor re-adds essential ones that were skipped.
Findings must point at real diff lines; shaky high-severity ones go to a prosecutor, defender and judge debate.
Three scorers vote only when the first score card is borderline; a non-AI calibrator can only make the verdict stricter.
Small models handle the default work, large ones only on evidence of risk, while a cost ledger skips optional work past a cap.
summary.stealThis: Before your next review agent, validate every finding against the diff (file and nearby line) in plain code and only send high-severity, low-confidence findings to a prosecutor/defender/judge debate.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're building a multi-agent PR reviewer, especially in Java or Quarkus, and want patterns for cost caps, escalation and failure handling.
summary.quote: What made them work together was not using any of them everywhere, but each one only where it pays off

verdict.reason: Teaches portable review-agent patterns with code, real cost, and an honest walkthrough of a 2900-line PR: deterministic validation of findings against diff lines, debate only for high-severity low-confidence findings, voting only on borderline scores, a calibrator that can only tighten verdicts, and a cost cap; the framework is Quarkus-specific but the ideas transfer.

summary.title: How to Write SKILL.md Files in Claude for Non-Coding Work (With a Real Test)
summary.idea: Repeated corrections to rough Claude drafts waste messages and tokens, so encode business tasks as SKILL.md files built from four blocks: trigger header, intake guard, numbered steps, and a checkable quality gate.
howItWorks: Write the YAML description around the output's shape and the exact moment in the workday to use it.
Add a short intake guard so Claude asks for missing facts like price or timeline instead of inventing them.
Use a fixed numbered execution sequence so the build order never changes between runs.
End with falsifiable quality checks: banned filler words, no 'not just X, it's Y' phrasing, concrete numbers in every bullet.
Claude loads only each skill's name and description up front, then pulls the full file when a request matches.
summary.stealThis: Before your next client proposal, create a skill with a three-fact intake check and a banned-words quality gate, then run it on a 24-word note to see if one turn is enough.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're a non-engineer or freelancer who keeps retyping the same corrections to Claude and wants a complete, copyable skill file to adapt.
summary.quote: Good rules are falsifiable: you can check pass or fail in five seconds by eye.

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable SKILL.md structure for non-coding work (trigger description, intake guard so the agent asks instead of inventing, numbered steps, falsifiable quality gate), with a full file, a free MIT repo and a real test run, though it carries Gumroad upsells and only one test example.

summary.title: GetMintOrg/Engineering: Guardrails for AI coding agents
summary.idea: Rules written in prose (CLAUDE.md) get broken eventually, so when you correct an agent twice on the same thing, turn the rule into a hook, lint rule or CI check that makes the mistake impossible.
howItWorks: A PreToolUse hook blocks writes to .env files, keys and credentials before the agent touches them.
A new-test hook requires a @guards tag naming the failure the test catches, and exit code 2 sends the reason back to the agent.
Custom oxlint rules ban mocking your own modules, narration comments and hand-rolled sleep delays.
A CI ratchet fails PRs that loosen lint budgets, grow exemption lists or add new disable directives.
A ship skill takes a change to a green PR with every review thread handled.
summary.stealThis: The next time you correct your agent twice for the same mistake, replace the CLAUDE.md line with a PreToolUse hook that exits 2 with a reason, like requiring a @guards comment on new test files.
summary.goDeeperIf: you're repeating the same corrections to your coding agent and want ready-made hooks, lint rules and CI checks to copy.
summary.quote: A rule in prose is a rule the agent will eventually break.

verdict.reason: A ready-to-copy repo that turns repeated prose corrections into enforcement: PreToolUse hooks that exit 2 with a reason (protect-files, @guards tags on new tests), custom oxlint rules, a CI lint ratchet and ship/dlq skills, with config snippets for each, matching the card's claims.
